New since the last digest

  • First Circuit revives an as-applied challenge to the federal felon-in-possession ban. On Friday, Nov. 13, a unanimous First Circuit panel, in an opinion by Chief Judge David Barron, vacated the dismissal of Thomas Marshall's civil suit in Marshall v. Blanche, No. 25-1721, and remanded for further proceedings. Marshall, of New Hampshire, is barred under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1) based on prior DUI convictions. This is not a ruling that § 922(g)(1) is unconstitutional; the law remains in force and the merits are undecided. item.title: First Circuit Revives New Hampshire Man's Challenge to Federal Felon Gun Ban in Marshall v. Blanche, Says 2011 Torres-Rosario Precedent No Longer Controls
item.description:
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, revived a New Hampshire man's Second Amendment challenge to the federal felon-in-possession ban, 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1). In Marshall v. Blanche, No. 25-1721, a unanimous panel, in an opinion by Chief Judge David Barron, vacated the dismissal of Thomas Marshall's civil suit and remanded for further proceedings. Marshall is barred based on prior DUI convictions. The court said its 2011 precedent, United States v. Torres-Rosario, no longer controls.

Why it matters: Federal appeals courts are split on whether people with felony convictions may bring individual, as-applied challenges to § 922(g)(1). The decision is not a ruling that the law is unconstitutional; the law remains in force and the merits are undecided.

item.title: Florida AG Uthmeier: State Bump-Stock Ban Violates the Second Amendment, Office Will Not Defend Convictions
item.description:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier released an opinion today, November 13, 2026, on whether the bump-fire stock prohibition in section 790.222, Florida Statutes, violates the Second Amendment. His answer: "After careful consideration, I have determined that it does."

Section 790.222 was passed in 2018 by the Florida Legislature and signed by then-Governor Rick Scott as part of the Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School Public Safety Act. The law makes it a third-degree felony to import, transfer, distribute, sell, keep for sale, offer for sale, possess or give to another person a bump-fire stock. In a post on X, Uthmeier said people are being arrested and prosecuted under the law, and that "the overly broad law appears to restrict the use of trigger enhancements used by firearms owners for lawful purposes, subjecting them to five years in prison."

The opinion applies the Supreme Court's Bruen test. It says semiautomatic firearms with bump stocks and similar modifications "are bearable arms covered by the Second Amendment's plain text," and that "No identifiable historical tradition justifies prohibiting their possession and use by law-abiding citizens for sporting, defensive, or other lawful purposes." Citing Garland v. Cargill, it notes that a rifle with a bump stock still fires only one round per function of the trigger and is not a machinegun.

The conclusion is direct: "Section 790.222 therefore violates the Second Amendment and cannot be lawfully enforced by Executive Branch officials in Florida. This Office will not defend a conviction under section 790.222."

What it means: an Attorney General opinion does not repeal the statute. Per the Florida Attorney General's own FAQ, "Opinions of the Attorney General, however, are not law. They are advisory only and are not binding in a court of law." Section 790.222 stays on the books until the Legislature changes it or a court strikes it down. The opinion is the state's chief legal officer saying the law is unconstitutional and that his office will not defend convictions under it.

Sources:

  • Attorney General James Uthmeier on X, with the full opinion (Nov 13, 2026)
  • Florida Attorney General, "Frequently Asked Questions About Attorney General Opinions"

item.title: Senate Judiciary meets Nov 17 on 14 nominees, including DOJ's Jesus Osete for Missouri federal bench
item.description:
The Senate Judiciary Committee has scheduled an executive business meeting for Tuesday, Nov 17, 2026 at 9:00 a.m. ET. The agenda lists 14 nominees: six judges (one for the Eighth Circuit and five for district courts), three U.S. Attorneys, four U.S. Marshals and one Parole Commission member.

One of them is Jesus A. Osete, nominated to be U.S. District Judge for the Western District of Missouri, replacing retiring Judge David Gregory Kays. Osete became Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights in August 2025. That division houses DOJ's Second Amendment Section. His name appears on DOJ gun-rights filings, including the December 2025 lawsuit against the District of Columbia and a brief arguing New Jersey's AR-15 and magazine bans violate the Second Amendment.

This is a business meeting, where the committee can vote nominees to the Senate floor, not a hearing. Osete had his hearing on Sept 30. All 14 nominees were on the Nov 10 agenda and were held over for a week under Committee Rule I.3, which puts them in line for a committee vote Tuesday. The committee can still delay.

The National Association for Gun Rights and the American Suppressor Association both sent the committee letters supporting Osete. AmmoLand News confirmed his nomination through the White House and the Senate nominations list. It was sent to the Senate Sept 14 and is still pending in committee.

item.title: Craig Trainor named acting head of DOJ Civil Rights Division, home of the Second Amendment Section
item.description:
Attorney General Todd Blanche announced on Nov 10, 2026 that President Trump appointed Craig Trainor as Acting Assistant Attorney General for the DOJ Civil Rights Division. Since October 2025, Trainor has served as HUD's Senate-confirmed Assistant Secretary for Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity. The Senate confirmed him to that post 51 to 47. Before HUD, he was acting assistant secretary for civil rights at the Education Department.

Trainor succeeds Harmeet Dhillon, who resigned Nov 5 after creating the division's first Second Amendment Section. Jesus Osete had been serving as acting head. The section, led by Acting Chief Barry Arrington, has sued over gun laws in D.C., Virginia and California, and AmmoLand reports several of those suits remain pending.

No public statement from Trainor on the Second Amendment or the section's future has been identified. It is unclear whether he will be nominated for the job permanently. As of midday Nov 11, DOJ's Civil Rights page still listed Osete as acting head.

item.title: Ohio House committee reports Sub. SB 214 on suppressors and sawed-off firearms (not law)
item.description:
What's new (as of Nov. 10, 2026 ET): The Ohio House Public Safety Committee held a third hearing today on Sen. Kyle Koehler’s S.B. 214 (136th General Assembly, 2025–2026). The official legislature site now lists the current version as Sub. S.B. 214, As Reported by the House Public Safety Committee. The Nov. 10 House calendar had the bill up for third consideration at 2:00 p.m. marked “Pending Committee Report.” As of this check, official votes and the LIS bill record still show no House floor vote, no “As Passed by the House” text, no Senate concurrence, and no presentation to or signature by Gov. DeWine. The bill is not law.

What the House-reported substitute would do: Its long title is “to amend sections 1533.04, 2923.11, 2923.12, and 2923.17 of the Revised Code to remove firearm mufflers and suppressors and sawed-off firearms from the classification of dangerous ordnance.” Compared with the Senate-passed text (which addressed mufflers/suppressors only), the House substitute also strikes “sawed-off firearm” from the R.C. 2923.11 “dangerous ordnance” definition, deletes the 2923.11(F) definition of “sawed-off firearm,” and makes conforming edits, including striking the hunting-law proviso in R.C. 1533.04 that had tied suppressor use while hunting to state/federal authorization and National Firearms Act registration, and striking a related R.C. 2923.17 exemption. The committee hearing materials list amendment AM_136_3310 (sponsored in the LIS record by Rep. Kevin D. Miller).

Prior official actions: Introduced in the Senate June 3, 2025; reported by Senate Armed Services, Veterans Affairs and Public Safety on March 11, 2026 (5–0 favorable); passed the Senate March 25, 2026, 31–1 (Sen. Beth Liston voting no); introduced in the House March 31, 2026; referred to House Public Safety on May 13, 2026. Earlier House hearings were June 2 and June 9, 2026.

Caveats: Because the House committee changed the Senate bill, House floor passage would still have to be followed by Senate concurrence before the measure could go to the Governor. This is a proposed change to Ohio’s dangerous-ordnance classification, not a change to federal law. The Legislative Service Commission’s as-introduced analysis of the suppressor provisions noted that, even if Ohio no longer treated a muffler or suppressor as dangerous ordnance, federal National Firearms Act registration would still be required.

Sources: Ohio Legislature – S.B. 214 (136th GA); As Reported by House Public Safety Committee (PDF); official votes; Nov. 10 Public Safety hearing.

item.title: 2d Cir. in Mills partly vacates dismissal of NYC handgun-rule challenges; affirms fees and standing
item.description:
What's new (as of Nov. 10, 2026 ET): The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit today issued a published opinion in Mills v. New York City, No. 24-3308-cv (argued Nov. 18, 2025; decided Nov. 10, 2026). The panel—Circuit Judges Raggi, Livingston, and Park, opinion by Judge Reena Raggi—reviewed a Dec. 5, 2024 judgment of the Southern District of New York (Rakoff, J.) that dismissed, in full, a complaint raising Second Amendment challenges to New York City handgun rules. Disposition: AFFIRMED IN PART; VACATED AND REMANDED IN PART. There is no separate concurrence or dissent. This is an appeal from a motion-to-dismiss judgment—not a preliminary-injunction ruling and not a final merits holding that any challenged rule is unconstitutional.

Opinion: https://ww3.ca2.uscourts.gov/decisions/OPN/24-3308_opn.pdf

Vacated and remanded (Bruen step one only): The court held that three challenges should not have been dismissed under Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(6) at Bruen step one, because the regulated conduct is covered by the Second Amendment’s plain text (or, for the waiting period, “meaningfully constrain[s]” that right). Those claims are remanded for Bruen step two—whether the City can show consistency with the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation. The court expressly did not decide that the rules are unconstitutional, and it declined to predict how step two will come out (slip op. at 3–4, 28–29, 38–40 & n.20):

  • 38 R.C.N.Y. § 5-22(a)(7) — limit of one handgun carried on the person at a time;
  • N.Y.C. Admin. Code § 10-302.1(a)–(b) — 90-day limit on acquiring more than one handgun;
  • 38 R.C.N.Y. § 5-25(d)(4) (repealed 2024) — former limit of two handguns registered on a carry license (the City told the district court the 2024 replacement no longer strictly imposes that cap; the remanded claim concerns the repealed rule).

Affirmed:

County enforcement of Bill 23-26E is not preliminarily blocked by this opinion. item.title: Florida AG: No NFA Paperwork Needed for Lawful SBR and SBS Possession Under State Law
item.description:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier issued statewide enforcement guidance on November 6, 2026, saying law-abiding Floridians do not need NFA approval, registration, or a federal tax stamp to lawfully possess short-barreled rifles and short-barreled shotguns under Florida law.

The memo addresses Florida Statutes section 790.221. That law generally prohibits possession of a short-barreled rifle, short-barreled shotgun, or machine gun, but contains an exception for firearms lawfully owned and possessed under federal law. Uthmeier says the statute does not independently criminalize possession of an SBR or SBS that a person may lawfully own and possess under federal law.

The guidance takes effect immediately and is expressly conditioned on no taxes being imposed on SBRs and SBSs. It says possession of an SBR or SBS alone does not provide reasonable suspicion or probable cause for a search or seizure. Finding one during an otherwise lawful encounter does not, by itself, justify a plain-view evidentiary seizure. Uthmeier also says his office will not defend a conviction under section 790.221 on appeal when the sole basis is the absence of NFA approval, registration, or a federal tax stamp.

The federal developments cited in the memo are not new today. An August 5, 2026 judgment in Silencer Shop Foundation v. ATF granted relief to specified plaintiffs and covered groups, not a nationwide injunction. ATF subsequently announced a nationwide non-enforcement policy for certain NFA approval and registration requirements in an October 9 open letter. That enforcement policy is not a repeal of the NFA.

Other restrictions remain. The memo says prohibited-person rules, dealer-transfer requirements, and applicable location restrictions still apply. Prior ATF authorization on Form 20 remains required for interstate transportation of SBRs and SBSs, and travelers must follow other states' laws. The NFA requirements for machine guns and destructive devices remain in place.

Today's development is statewide Attorney General enforcement guidance interpreting existing Florida law. It is not a new statute or a court ruling striking down section 790.221.

  • Florida Statutes § 790.221

item.title: DOJ Gun-Rights Restoration Portal Hits 5,000-Applicant Cap, Closed Until January 2027
item.description:
DOJ's federal gun-rights restoration portal hit its 5,000-applicant cap on its first public day and is closed to new applications until January 2027.

Why it matters: 925(c) relief went unused for more than 30 years because Congress stopped funding it. This first public window filled in about a day, which shows how much demand there is and how narrow the program is for now. Federal relief does not lift a separate state firearm ban.

item.title: Sixth Circuit Upholds Federal Mental-Health Gun Ban in U.S. v. Laykovich
item.description:
Sixth Circuit upholds federal mental-health gun ban, 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(4), against a Second Amendment challenge (verified: opinion on the court's site).

In United States v. Laykovich, No. 25-5766 (6th Cir., published opinion 26a0293p.06, decided and filed Oct. 29, 2026), a panel of Judges Gibbons, Murphy and Hermandorfer affirmed a conviction under § 922(g)(4), which bars gun possession by anyone "adjudicated as a mental defective" or "committed to a mental institution." Judge Eric Murphy wrote the opinion; no dissent.

The court rejected Laykovich's facial Second Amendment challenge. It held that, at least as applied to him, the ban is "relevantly similar" under Bruen to historical laws allowing civil detention of people whose mental illness made them dangerous, because it serves the same public-safety purpose and lasts only until he shows he no longer poses a threat. Laykovich had been involuntarily committed by a Missouri court in 2023 and was stopped in Kentucky in 2024 wearing body armor with eight firearms, en route to Fort Knox. His separate sentencing claims were also rejected.

Why it matters: This is a published circuit precedent keeping § 922(g)(4) enforceable in Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio and Tennessee, and it is likely to be cited in other circuits. The opinion distinguishes the Supreme Court's narrower treatment of § 922(g)(3) in Hemani. It did not reach how the ban applies to people with older or less clear-cut commitments. The ruling came out Oct. 29 but was first reported publicly today.

Sources:

item.title: DOJ: ATF employees will serve as Nov. 3 election monitors
item.description:

According to the filing, the monitors will be unarmed, won't wear ATF insignia (they've been told to wear business casual), and can't make arrests. Why it matters: It's unclear whether ATF staff have ever been used for DOJ election monitoring before. item.title: Judge refuses to enter agreed judgment striking Florida's gun waiting period (Dunn v. Glass)
item.description:

item.title: DOJ finalizes rule letting FFLs run voluntary NICS checks on employees (BSCA firearm-handler checks)
item.description:
DOJ finalizes rule letting gun dealers run voluntary NICS checks on employees (verified: Federal Register public inspection, filed Mon Oct 26, 2026 8:45 AM ET; publishes Tue Oct 27).

What is new: DOJ/FBI has filed a final rule, "Bipartisan Safer Communities Act of 2022 – Criteria for NICS Background Checks of Firearm Handlers" (FR Doc. 2026-21920; 28 CFR Part 25; RIN 1110-AA35; Docket FBI-159). It lets federal firearms licensees (FFLs) voluntarily use NICS to run "firearm handler background checks" on current or prospective employees who can access firearms, ammunition, or their manufacturing components. It takes effect 30 days after publication (about Nov. 26, 2026). It was signed Oct. 22 by Attorney General Todd Blanche.

  • The checks are voluntary for FFLs, and the employee must give informed, written consent first. State point-of-contact agencies don't have to process them unless they opt in.
  • The final rule mostly tracks the Dec. 12, 2024 proposal (89 FR 100424), which drew 25 comments. One change: "eligible employee" now also covers independent contractors or agents who work on the licensee's premises with access to guns, ammo, or components (added after NSSF comments).
  • ATF dropped the proposed Form 5300.47. It has instead proposed using a revised Form 4473 for these checks, with a 90-day records-retention period. Until that's final, ATF says it will issue guidance on using the current 4473.

Why it matters: This is the employee-screening piece of the 2022 BSCA (34 U.S.C. 40901(b)(2)) finally becoming operative. It's a new NICS use outside of gun sales, and it ties into ATF's pending Form 4473 revision.

item.title: DOJ opens Second Amendment probe of Waterbury and Middletown, Conn., carry-permit delays
item.description:
DOJ opens Second Amendment pattern-or-practice probe of Waterbury and Middletown, Conn., carry-permit handling (verified, DOJ press release and notice letters dated Thu Oct 22, 2026).

What's new: The Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, through its Second Amendment Section, notified the City of Waterbury and the Town of Middletown and their police departments that it is investigating whether they unnecessarily delay or deny permits to carry a firearm. The letters say DOJ has reached no conclusions and asked each city to name a contact within five business days. AAG Harmeet Dhillon announced it on X Thursday afternoon.

DOJ again relies on Bruen's warning against "lengthy wait times in processing license applications." If DOJ finds reasonable cause, it can publish findings, seek an agreement, or sue in federal district court. Connecticut's Board of Firearms Permit Examiners appeal backlog (1,203 pending cases as of March 2024 per a state audit, as reported by CT Insider) is the context.

item.title: Cook County and Connecticut file SCOTUS briefs defending AR-15 bans (Viramontes / Grant)
item.description:
What's new (verified on the SCOTUS docket): Cook County and Connecticut submitted their merits briefs on Wed., Oct. 21, 2026 (about 5:20 PM ET) in Viramontes v. Cook County, No. 25-238, consolidated with Grant v. Higgins, No. 25-566, the AR-15 ban cases set for argument Dec. 2, 2026. The docket lists both briefs as "submitted," not yet formally filed.

  • Cook County (State's Attorney Eileen O'Neill Burke, counsel of record) argues the county ordinance fits a historical tradition of regulating "unusually dangerous weapons," that the ordinance responds to dangers created by technological change, and that a weapon's popularity does not shield it from regulation. It also argues AR-15s are not in common use for any purpose that immunizes them.
  • Connecticut (AG William Tong's office, with former U.S. Solicitor General Elizabeth Prelogar of Cooley LLP as counsel of record) frames the question as whether the Second and Fourteenth Amendments guarantee a right to possess AR-15 platform rifles, argues English and state laws regulated unusually dangerous weapons, that AR-15s are unusually dangerous, and that petitioners' "common-use-only" test lacks merit.

Why it matters: These are the states' main defense of AR-15 bans before the Court's first merits case on the issue. Petitioners' reply is next; the United States has already filed in support of petitioners and asked for argument time.

Unverified: SAF (@2AFDN) is live-threading the briefs on X and says Cook County no longer disputes that AR-15s are "arms"; that's SAF's reading, not checked against the full brief.

item.title: Federal judge strikes down New York body armor ban (Heeter v. James), 14-day stay
item.description:
What's new (verified, primary source): On Oct 21, 2026, U.S. District Judge John L. Sinatra Jr. (W.D.N.Y.) granted summary judgment to the plaintiffs in Heeter v. James, No. 1:24-cv-00623 (Benjamin Heeter, Joseph Wurtenberg and Firearms Policy Coalition). He held that New York's ban on the purchase and sale of body armor by people outside eligible professions (N.Y. Penal Law §§ 270.21 and 270.22, Gen. Bus. Law § 396-eee) violates the Second Amendment.

Relief: The court permanently enjoined the named defendants (the NY Attorney General, the State Police superintendent, and the Erie and Monroe County district attorneys) from enforcing the ban as to sale and purchase. The judge rejected the State's argument that Trump v. CASA bars statewide relief. He also granted the State's request for a 14-day stay pending appeal, so the injunction is not yet in effect. The State's cross-motions were denied on this issue.

Key reasoning: The court found body armor is an "arm" under Heller's definition and is in common use for lawful purposes. It said the State identified no well-established historical tradition supporting the ban and offered no evidence that body armor, which the court called a purely defensive arm, is "uniquely designed to create mayhem" under the Second Circuit's Lamont standard. That standard is now before the Supreme Court as Grant v. Higgins, set for argument Dec 2.

Why it matters: The court called New York's law "first-of-its-kind," and this is a final judgment on the merits rather than a preliminary ruling. An appeal to the Second Circuit is expected but not yet filed (unverified), and the 14-day stay gives the State time to seek a longer one.

Sources: Decision and Order, Dkt. 95 (PDF) · FPC case page · CourtListener docket · SAF post

item.title: Mass. SJC upholds age-21 minimum for a license to carry in Commonwealth v. Thomson
item.description:
Mass. SJC upholds age-21 minimum for a license to carry (Commonwealth v. Thomson, SJC-13856), decided Tue Oct 20, 2026

What is new (verified from the slip opinion): Massachusetts' highest court rejected a Second Amendment challenge to the rule that a person must be at least 21 to get a license to carry (G.L. c. 140, § 131(d)) and affirmed Mikai Thomson's conviction for carrying a firearm without a license (G.L. c. 269, § 10(a)). Thomson was 20 when police found a loaded 9mm in December 2021; the case was argued March 2, 2026.

  • Holding: Opinion by Justice Wolohojian. The court said restricting firearm possession by those deemed too young to handle them safely outside supervised settings "is consistent with the nation's regulatory tradition." It analogized the age-21 license rule to the founding-era practice of parents or other responsible adults supplying arms to under-21s for supervised militia use, citing the Eleventh Circuit's en banc NRA v. Bondi.
  • Standing: Because Thomson never applied for a license, he could not bring an as-applied challenge, but he could bring a facial one. The court left open a "futility" route to as-applied standing in a future case with a proper record.
  • Split bench: Justice Kafker, joined by Justice Wendlandt, concurred in part and dissented in part. They agreed Thomson could raise the facial challenge but would have required more briefing and expert historical analysis instead of the court drawing the historical analogy itself.

Why it matters: This is a state high court ruling on the federal Second Amendment that keeps the 18–20 carry-license bar in place in Massachusetts. It sits against federal appeals rulings that struck down 18–20 restrictions (Lara, 3d Cir.; Worth, 8th Cir.; Reese, 5th Cir.), which the opinion discusses, and alongside Bondi, which upheld one. Because it decides a federal constitutional question, a U.S. Supreme Court cert petition is possible. None has been filed, and that would be speculation for now.

Not yet verified: There's no press coverage yet, no statement from the defense or gun-rights groups, and no word on whether a cert petition is planned.

Sources: SJC slip opinion (mass.gov) · CourtListener copy · Background on the March 2 argument (Boston Lawyer Blog)

item.title: SCOTUS denies cert in Beckwith v. Frey; Maine's 72-hour firearm waiting period stays in place
item.description:
STATUS: MATERIAL_NEW

SCOTUS denies cert in Beckwith v. Frey; Maine's 72-hour firearm waiting period stays in place

What's new (verified, Supreme Court order list, Mon Oct 19, 2026): The Court denied certiorari in Beckwith v. Frey, No. 26-258, the challenge to Maine's 72-hour waiting period on firearm purchases. It appears in the plain "certiorari denied" list with no noted dissent and no statement from any Justice. The petition had been distributed for the Oct 16 conference.

Background: Maine's 2024 law requires most buyers to wait 72 hours after purchase before taking possession of a firearm. The First Circuit (No. 25-1160, decided Apr 3, 2026) vacated a district-court preliminary injunction against the law. Per the cert petition, the First Circuit reasoned that laws regulating acquisition don't implicate the Second Amendment unless they are "abusive," and the petition argued this conflicts with the Tenth Circuit's ruling against New Mexico's 7-day waiting period.

Why it matters: The denial leaves the First Circuit's decision in place, and the disagreement the petitioners described between the First and Tenth Circuits on waiting periods remains unresolved by the Court. A cert denial is not a ruling on the merits, and the case came up in a preliminary-injunction posture.

Also on today's list: No other Second Amendment cases were granted or denied. Novotny v. Moore (No. 25-1324) was rescheduled off the Oct 16 conference on Oct 13, so no action was expected, and Duncan v. Bonta (No. 25-198) remains pending with no action.

item.title: En banc Third Circuit: felon gun ban unconstitutional as applied to decades-old DUI offender (Williams)
item.description:
STATUS: MATERIAL_NEW

What's new (verified, primary opinion): The en banc Third Circuit decided Williams v. Attorney General, No. 24-1091, on Oct. 13, 2026, and affirmed summary judgment for Edward Williams, holding 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1) unconstitutional as applied to him. Williams's predicate was a 2005 Pennsylvania DUI at the highest BAC tier that, as a second offense, was punishable by up to five years; he served his sentence on home confinement. This is the companion case flagged as still pending when the court decided United States v. Bost earlier the same day.

  • Majority: Judge Matey, joined by Judges Hardiman, Bibas, Porter, Phipps, Bove and Mascott. The court read the historical tradition as permitting disarmament of people who pose a risk of physical violence, not felons as a class, and said the government had not shown Williams is currently dangerous.
  • § 925(c) argument rejected: The majority declined DOJ's request to make Williams first use the newly revived administrative rights-restoration process (91 FR 54054). In the court's words: "Our duty is to decide the case based on present facts, not future promises."
  • Lineup: Chief Judge Chagares concurred in the judgment but would generally require people to go through § 925(c) first (he excused Williams given the case's long history). Judge Freeman (with Judges Montgomery-Reeves and Chung) and Judge Shwartz (with Judges Krause and Restrepo) dissented from the judgment. By our count of the listed lineup, that is 8–6 to affirm.

Why it matters: Read with Bost (same court, same day, upholding § 922(g)(1) for a terroristic-threats predicate), the Third Circuit now has an en banc framework where violent predicates support disarmament and a non-violent, decades-old DUI predicate does not. It also squarely addresses whether § 925(c) relief displaces as-applied court challenges, a question DOJ has been pressing in other circuits. The relief is a declaratory judgment specific to Williams, not a nationwide ruling. Possible next steps are a government cert petition or acceptance; neither has been announced.

Background (not new): Bost (3d Cir. en banc, No. 24-1719) and SCOTUS's Oct. 13 cert denial in Johnson v. United States, No. 26-270, were briefed earlier today.

Third Circuit en banc opinion, Williams v. Attorney General, No. 24-1091 (PDF)
Same-day companion opinion, United States v. Bost, No. 24-1719 (PDF)

item.description:
Verified. The Ninth Circuit today published United States v. Youngblood, No. 24-7629 (Tallman, Owens, R. Nelson; filed Oct. 13, 2026), affirming a §922(g)(3) conviction of a frequent methamphetamine and fentanyl user.

The panel held that its earlier ruling that §922(g)(3) is facially constitutional (United States v. Stennerson, 2025) remains binding after the Supreme Court’s United States v. Hemani (2026). Hemani resolved a narrow as-applied challenge (marijuana use “about every other day”) and left open present-intoxication applications; the panel found Stennerson not “clearly irreconcilable” with Hemani. It also held Youngblood waived his as-applied challenge by failing to argue it specifically in his opening brief.

Why it matters: Among the first published circuit opinions on how much of §922(g)(3)’s facial validity survives Hemani; binding across the Ninth Circuit.

item.title: En Banc Third Circuit Upholds Felon Gun Ban for Violent Offender in U.S. v. Bost
item.description:
Verified. The en banc Third Circuit today affirmed the felon-in-possession conviction in United States v. Bost, No. 24-1719 (precedential, filed Oct. 13, 2026).

Judge Bibas wrote for the majority: some predicate crimes, including Pennsylvania terroristic threats, show “a prima facie risk of physical violence from misusing guns,” so people convicted of those crimes “may presumptively be disarmed based on those convictions alone.” Joining Bibas: Chief Judge Chagares and Judges Hardiman, Porter, Matey, Freeman, and Fisher (Montgomery-Reeves joined except Section II.B; Mascott joined only Part I, Section II.A, and Part IV). Shwartz (with Krause and Restrepo) concurred in the judgment on a broader theory that all felonies can disarm. Mascott would uphold the ban as applied to Bost but not categorically by offense class. Phipps dissented, joined by Bove, and would find § 922(g)(1) unconstitutional as applied to Bost.

Why it matters: First en banc Third Circuit felon-in-possession ruling since the Range decisions, under a more conservative court. It sets a “violent predicate → presumptively disarmed” frame that diverges from the Fifth Circuit’s as-applied approach (e.g., Hembree on simple drug possession), deepening the circuit split over how Rahimi applies to felons and keeping the issue in front of SCOTUS. Reargued en banc Feb. 11, 2026 together with Williams v. Attorney General (old DUI predicate); Williams is not decided yet. Opinion is 61 pages with five separate writings.

Primary source: Third Circuit opinion PDF. Coverage: Bloomberg Law.

item.title: ATF releases NFA guidance: no approval or registration required for suppressors, SBRs, SBSs and AOWs, for everyone
item.description:
STATUS: MATERIAL_NEW

ATF releases its post-Hendrix NFA guidance: as of today, Oct 9, 2026, ATF says it will no longer require approval or registration for suppressors, SBRs, SBSs and AOWs, for everyone, not just the Silencer Shop plaintiffs.

Hook: No Form 4, no Form 1, no registry. ATF Director Robert Cekada's open letter says ATF is extending the Silencer Shop non-enforcement to every American as a matter of enforcement discretion. But it's discretion, not a repeal, and state law still controls.

What ATF actually said (Open Letter to All FFLs and the Public, dated Oct 9, 2026, digitally signed by Director Cekada at 11:11 AM ET; reports surfaced publicly about 3:17 PM ET):

"Although the district court's injunction applies only to plaintiffs and certain other specified persons, the Department has determined to exercise its enforcement discretion to create greater uniformity, consistent with the Attorney General's statement today. Consequently, effective October 9, 2026, ATF will no longer require individuals to seek ATF approval under the NFA before making or transferring short-barreled rifles, short-barreled shotguns, silencers, and "any other weapon[s]" as defined in 26 U.S.C. § 5845(e). ATF will also no longer require such items to be registered in the National Firearms Registration and Transfer Record. These policies apply uniformly to anyone otherwise subject to these requirements, not just to the plaintiffs in the litigation."
"ATF will continue to administer the NFA on a voluntary basis. ATF will accept Form 1 applications to make or register these firearms and devices by those making such items. ATF will also accept Form 3 or Form 4 applications to transfer or register such items."

Primary document: ATF open letter (atf.gov PDF). A companion 24-question FAQ accompanies it.

What changes for transfers, tax stamps and registration

  • Form 4 and Form 1: No longer required to make or transfer a suppressor, SBR, SBS or AOW. Both can still be filed voluntarily, and ATF will keep approving them.
  • Form 3 (dealer to dealer): ATF "will not require such forms" for interstate FFL-to-FFL sales of silencers and AOWs (FAQ 13). Voluntary filing is still allowed.
  • At the counter: FFLs process these items like any other GCA firearm, meaning a Form 4473, a NICS check, and normal records, with the usual in-state-resident limits (FAQ 9, 12).
  • Registration: NFRTR registration is no longer required. ATF will keep the registry for voluntary registrations. Dealers can ask ATF's NFA Division to remove items already transferred on a 4473, and people can withdraw pending applications or unregister items, but ATF warns that once removed, an item "cannot be re-registered unless the Attorney General declares an amnesty" (FAQ 18, 22).
  • Tax stamps: The making and transfer tax on these items was already $0 under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Special occupational taxes (SOT) for businesses that manufacture, import or deal in NFA items still apply.
  • Other NFA rules ATF will stop enforcing for these items: the 24-hour registration rule for manufacturers, the NFA marking requirement, the bans on making, receiving, transferring or possessing unregistered items (except obliterated-serial and illegally imported items), and the ban on interstate transport of unregistered items under 26 U.S.C. § 5861(j) (FAQ 8, 17, 20).
  • SBRs and SBSs specifically: The GCA still requires Attorney General authorization for an FFL to sell an SBR or SBS (18 U.S.C. § 922(b)(4)), and no non-NFA process exists yet. ATF says it is drafting forms and regulations and "will not enforce 18 U.S.C. § 922(b)(4)" in the meantime. A Form 20 is still required before taking an SBR or SBS across state lines, even if it's unregistered (FAQ 15, 21).

Who it covers: Anyone otherwise subject to the NFA, whether or not they're a plaintiff, member or customer covered by the Silencer Shop injunction, but only for the $0-tax items (suppressors, SBRs, SBSs, AOWs). Machine guns and destructive devices keep the $200 tax and every NFA requirement. Prohibited persons still can't possess any of these items, since they remain GCA "firearms."

Caveats

  • This is enforcement discretion, not a rule change or a court ruling. ATF's FAQ says enforcement could resume if Congress adds a new tax, the injunction is dissolved or overturned, or DOJ rescinds the policy. It says unregistered NFA items are treated as contraband with felony penalties, and that there is no automatic grandfathering. An amnesty would be the Attorney General's call (FAQ 23, 24).
  • State law is untouched. ATF says most states have NFA possession laws tied to federal registration, and ATF "cannot opine" on whether unregistered items qualify under those laws. FFLs still can't transfer in violation of state or local law (18 U.S.C. § 922(b)(2)). ATF says it's unclear whether state courts will apply the § 926A travel safe harbor to unregistered items.
  • District court orders don't bind other courts, which could rule differently on the NFA's constitutionality (FAQ 7).

Still unclear

  • The letter cites "the Attorney General's statement today." I couldn't find that statement on DOJ's press release feed as of about 3:20 PM ET.
  • How this affects DOJ's Oct 12 response to the nine states' motion for clarification in Silencer Shop, and the Brown v. ATF (E.D. Mo.) case, where DOJ argued on Oct 7 against statewide or nationwide relief.
  • When ATF's new SBR/SBS transfer forms and regulations will come out.
  • atf.gov blocked automated access during this check. The letter text above was verified from the signed PDF (a copy posted by The Reload), and it matches the atf.gov link FPC posted and the quote NAGR posted.

What's new: On its Monday, Oct 5, 2026 order list, the Supreme Court denied the federal government's petition in United States v. Hembree, No. 25-1219, with no noted dissent. That leaves in place the Fifth Circuit's Jan 27, 2026 ruling (No. 24-60436) that 18 U.S.C. 922(g)(1), the federal felon-in-possession ban, violates the Second Amendment as applied to Charles Hembree, whose prior felony was simple drug possession (as described in press coverage of the ruling). Verified on the order list and the docket.

In April it asked the Court to hold the case for Hemani and then send it back to the Fifth Circuit to reconsider after that decision (a "grant, vacate and remand"). The Court instead denied outright after deciding Hemani in June, so the Fifth Circuit's as-applied 922(g)(1) ruling stands. The denial sets no national precedent, but the ruling remains binding in the Fifth Circuit (Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi), and the Court has once again passed on taking up 922(g)(1) after Hemani. Background: Hemani (June 18, 2026) held 922(g)(3), the drug-user ban, unconstitutional as applied, and Gorsuch's opinion expressly said it was not addressing felon disarmament.

Griffin), so two district courts now disagree on these bans. item.title: San Diego County sues filament maker Polymaker over ghost-gun marketing
item.description: STATUS: MATERIAL_NEW San Diego County sues 3D-printer filament maker Polymaker over ghost-gun marketing WHAT'S NEW: On Oct 5, 2026, San Diego County Counsel Damon Brown filed People v. Polymaker LLC in San Diego Superior Court. It's the County, not the City. GIFFORDS Law Center and White & Case are co-counsel. It was one of the first three suits from the County's new Consumer Fairness and Public Protection unit; the other two target AppLovin and Roblox. The case number was blank on the posted copy and is unverified. THE CLAIM: A single count under California's Unfair Competition Law (Bus. & Prof. Code 17200). The County's theory is that marketing filament for gun-making makes it a regulated "firearm precursor part" under Penal Code 16531. It alleges violations of the precursor-part sales laws, AB 1263's ban on knowingly facilitating illegal gun-making (Civ. Code 3273.625 / Penal Code 29186, effective Jan 1, 2026), and the Firearm Industry Responsibility Act. KEY ALLEGATIONS (none proven): - A "3D Print General PLA Pro" spool sold with YouTuber Sean Aranda's likeness and the slogan "Come and Make It." - Polymaker allegedly sponsored Aranda after YouTube demonetized him, then hired him in Dec 2023. He's now Head of Customer Experience and is not a defendant. - On r/fosscad, asked "Which is better for building guns?", Polymaker's account allegedly recommended PolyLite PLA Pro. - Polymaker's wiki allegedly calls J-B Weld "[p]opular in functional applications like 3D-printed firearms." - In May 2026, SDPD found Polymaker filament, four printed handgun frames and conversion devices at the home of an arrested 16-year-old. The complaint does not allege the marketing caused that purchase. WHAT THE COUNTY WANTS: Civil penalties up to $2,500 per violation (each day counted separately; no total stated), disgorgement of revenue tied to the marketing, injunctions, and attorney's fees. item.title: DOJ tells Fifth Circuit under-21 handgun case is moot, pledges no enforcement anywhere
item.description:
DOJ tells Fifth Circuit the under-21 handgun case is moot because it won't enforce the ban against anyone, anywhere (filed Mon Oct 5, 2026).

What's new: In FPC v. ATF (formerly Reese v. ATF; 5th Cir. No. 26-30154; W.D. La. No. 6:20-cv-01438), DOJ filed its brief on today's deadline arguing the appeal over the scope of the injunction is moot. DOJ cites the recent Office of Legal Counsel (OLC) opinion concluding the federal ban on licensed-dealer handgun sales to 18–20-year-olds is unconstitutional, and says DOJ "will not enforce the challenged provisions against anyone, anywhere." It argues in the alternative that, if the case isn't moot, the OLC opinion gives no basis to expand the injunction, and that ordinary Article III and equitable limits apply to associational plaintiffs.

Why it matters: The district court's injunction covers only FPC and Louisiana Shooting Association members who were members when the suit was filed and who live in the Fifth Circuit. FPC is asking the Fifth Circuit to extend relief to all current and future members, including outside the circuit. DOJ's non-enforcement pledge is a policy position that a future administration could reverse, while a broader injunction would be binding. So the fight is now over how far court-ordered relief reaches, not over whether the ban is constitutional (the Fifth Circuit already held it isn't).

Verification: The filing is reported and quoted by Bearing Arms (Cam Edwards, 3:31 PM ET). The primary brief has not been located publicly yet, so treat the quotes as reported, not independently verified.
